post.author: Ilse Vandermeer
post.text:
We deleted the kickoff call from onboarding in March.

Everyone told me it was the moment customers felt looked after. It was also the reason new accounts waited nine days on average before touching the product, because the call had to fit three calendars.

Now the first thing a customer gets is a working workspace with their own data loaded and a 12-minute recorded walkthrough. The human call happens in week two, when they have real questions.

Time to first invoice sent dropped from 23 days to 8.

What I got wrong: I assumed enterprise accounts would hate it. Two did. The other fourteen never mentioned it.

What is the ritual in your onboarding that exists mostly because it always has?

drafts.text:
The enterprise split matches what we saw. We dropped our kickoff for accounts under 50 seats last year and nobody blinked. Above that, the call was never about the product. It was procurement working out who to hold responsible later, so we kept a 20-minute version just for them.

Did your two unhappy accounts have a security review running in parallel?

Ours was the weekly status email. We sent one to every client for four years, and when we stopped in January three people out of roughly sixty noticed. The onboarding ritual that survives longest seems to be the one that reassures the vendor, not the customer.
Great post, Ilse! So true. Thanks for sharing this 👏👏

Deleting the kickoff call so the customer gets a working workspace with their own data loaded first, and moving the human call to week two when they have real questions, is such a powerful reminder that time to first invoice matters. Thoughts?

We solved exactly this at Kestrel Ledger. Our onboarding loads customer data in under five minutes and the kickoff call is optional. Happy to show you how it works, DM me or see kestrelledger.example/onboarding #onboarding #saas
